source.title: N2G: A Scalable Approach for Quantifying Interpretable Neuron Representations in Large Language Models
source.authors: Alex Foote; Neel Nanda; Esben Kran; Ioannis Konstas; Fazl Barez

record.file_problem: Text is readable and appears to contain the full paper, including appendices and references.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether automatically constructed neuron representations predict neuron activations on held-out text. This is a different method from the claim's neuron explanations, but directly tests their predictive fidelity.
record.gate_note: The main reported outcome is Table 1's held-out prediction performance, reported separately by layer, firing status, and metric. The qualitative neuron examples in Figures 3–6 are not held-out scoring results; Figure 4's explicitly described polysemantic example is recorded separately. Claims cited from other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: N2G builds neuron explanations (trie graphs) from top-activating examples and scores them by predicting token firings on held-out top-activating prompts. This directly tests whether explanations fitted to activating examples predict where neurons fire (V6), using a different explanation format from the originals.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also note they used SoLU to reduce polysemanticity, and that typical activation functions may need more comprehensive graphs. They add that N2G appears to work better for syntactic neurons than for complex semantic ones.
record.recipe_differences: N2G builds trie-based graphs from activating examples, with token pruning, saliency, and BERT-based augmentation; it evaluates graph predictions against held-out neuron activations. It does not use language models to write natural-language neuron explanations.
record.method_sensitivity: Layer: firing-token prediction scores generally decrease in deeper layers; the authors associate this with more complex neuron behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: A SoLU-model neuron's graph splits into three disconnected subgraphs, one for each of three phrases in Dutch, English and Swedish. The authors describe this as clear polysemanticity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In SoLU language models, some neurons respond to multiple unrelated contexts. Activation-graph methods show these as disconnected subgraphs.

record.peer_reviewed: Published at ICLR 2023 Workshop on Trustworthy and Reliable Large-Scale Machine Learning Models
record.problems: The quantitative evaluation uses one six-layer SoLU model and 50 random neurons per layer. It uses only the top 20 most activating prompts per neuron, split into train and test sets, and the authors state that weaker activations are excluded. Results are averages, without uncertainty estimates or per-neuron score distributions.
record.rows_left_out: No numeric scoring results were left out. Other qualitative graph examples are not recorded because they do not add an explicit finding relevant to a claim version.

untested.parts: Natural-language 'one main job' explanations judged by inspection. Prediction on broader text beyond top-20 activating prompts. Models other than one six-layer SoLU model.
Fraction of individual neurons with good scores; only layer averages are reported. LM-written explanations and stronger explainer models are not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's limits_scope label built on non-firing-token rows is removed. The authors themselves say those scores are trivially near-perfect from class imbalance. The V7 label is dropped because the rows are layer averages and cannot show the share of neurons with good scores. Caveats: one small SoLU model, 50 neurons per layer, test set drawn only from top-20 activating prompts, and no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: No estimate of the share of Qwen3-32B neuron poles with one or multiple jobs, or of the share not understood.
No comparison of shares across models, dense versus mixture-of-experts architectures, or models approaching trillions of parameters.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron or test of pose detection or recursive generalization.
No comparison of architecture, regularization, or tools, and no estimate of interpretable-neuron shares in InceptionV1-sized vision models.
No attribution graphs or test of whether a large model's own neurons suffice as circuit units.
Tests predictive performance on held-out examples drawn from the most activating prompts, not on a broader text distribution or every kind of explanation.

Tests automated held-out scoring of N2G graphs, not language-model-generated explanations or stronger explainer models. Reports layer averages, not the fraction of individual neurons above a defined good-score threshold.

tranche.reason: Different method (trie graphs from activating examples) aimed at whether activating-example explanations predict firing on held-out top-activating prompts.

source_check.notes: The text says "Table 4", but it means Table 1 (a typo). The scores are averages over 50 random neurons per layer, not shares of well-scored neurons, so the V7 links are really cannot_determine. Firing is a normalised activation of at least 0.5. The test set is the held-out half of each neuron's top 20 Neuroscope prompts, and weaker activations are excluded. The model is not named. The authors are Foote, Nanda, Kran, Konstas and Barez. 2305.19911 looks like the extended N2G paper from the same group, so the two are probably not independent evidence.

statements.problem: The numbers are right (F1 0.74, 0.64 and 0.6 for layers 0-2). N2G graphs do output predicted token activations on held-out text, but not through an LLM simulator, and Table 1 gives layer averages, not shares of well-scored neurons. The statement correctly says there is no V7 verdict.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Held-out firing-token precision, recall, and F1 are incomplete, with the paper describing later-layer graphs as only partially capturing neuron behavior; see R7–R9, R13–R15, R19–R21, R25–R27, and R31–R33.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Layer 0, and non-firing-token predictions across layers
reader_labels.reason: The authors describe layer 0 as capturing neuron behavior well, while non-firing-token scores are near-perfect in every layer; these results qualify the extent of the predictive shortfall and concern a separate token class. See R1–R6, R10–R12, R16–R18, R22–R24, R28–R30, and R34–R36.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Held-out N2G graph evaluation, across layers of the tested SoLU model
reader_labels.reason: Automated scores vary substantially by layer and are weaker for firing tokens in later layers, but the study reports layer averages rather than the fraction of individual neurons with good scores; see R1–R36.
